abstract: WSJ reports the launch of RAISE US, a bipartisan consortium designed to prepare the US workforce for AI-driven disruption. The group is led by former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo (CEO, served under President Biden) and former Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb (Republican). Founding employers include Amazon, Microsoft, Bank of America, and Eli Lilly. OpenAI and Anthropic are involved as AI-lab participants, and MIT economist David Autor sits on the advisory board. The organization has raised over $500 million — about half of its multiyear goal — from companies and nonprofits, and will initially partner with state governments in Arkansas, Maryland, Utah, and Connecticut. RAISE US frames its mandate as broader than traditional retraining: it intends to act as a working lab for testing workforce-transition policies, propose updates to decades-old programs like unemployment insurance (e.g., allowing displaced workers to keep benefits while launching AI-enabled businesses), and design corporate incentives for employers to hold on to workers whose roles are disrupted by AI and reskill them internally. Featured state initiatives include a Maryland service-year expansion targeting healthcare and an Arkansas AI-powered career navigation platform. Raimondo: 'There's an enormous amount of money and focus right now on winning the technology: the chips, the models. There's not enough attention on securing the future for the American worker.' Holcomb: 'The scale of change and reshaping of jobs and careers is different — and more so than it has ever been, I think, in human history.'
keyFindings: RAISE US is a bipartisan workforce-transition consortium launched June 25, 2026 — first large institutional response treating AI labor disruption as a policy problem rather than a technology problem
Led by Gina Raimondo (CEO, former Commerce Secretary) and Eric Holcomb (former Indiana Governor)
$500M+ raised — about half of multiyear fundraising goal — from companies and nonprofits
Founding employers: Amazon, Microsoft, Bank of America, Eli Lilly; AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic also involved
MIT economist David Autor sits on the advisory board
Initial state pilots: Arkansas (AI-powered career navigation platform), Maryland (service-year expansion targeting healthcare), Utah, Connecticut
Mandate explicitly includes revisiting unemployment insurance — e.g., letting displaced workers retain benefits while starting AI-enabled businesses
Plans to design corporate incentives for employers to retain and reskill workers whose roles AI disrupts, rather than lay off
Leadership Now Project (400+ current/retired executives) devoted spring 2026 sessions to AI's job impact, comparing scale to globalization/offshoring but framing it as larger
methodology: News reporting based on interviews with Raimondo, Holcomb, Microsoft's Brad Smith, and announcement materials. Tier 3 — journalism, not original empirical analysis. Authoritative on coalition composition, leadership, funding, and initial state partners; less authoritative on programmatic outcomes (the group has just launched).
qualifiers: Tier 3 news article — a coalition launch, not yet an outcomes study. Founding-employer list and $500M fundraising figure are reported by the organization itself, not independently audited. The first concrete state programs (Maryland service year, Arkansas career navigator) are scoping descriptions; results are not yet measurable. Notable structural asymmetry: founding employers (Amazon, Microsoft, BofA, Eli Lilly, OpenAI, Anthropic) include some of the same firms whose AI deployments are driving displacement signals tracked on jobsdata.ai — the coalition is, in effect, the displacers funding a partial response to displacement. This is consistent with cost-of-disruption being borne primarily by workers and states while platforms capture the productivity gains, a dynamic Acemoglu/Autor/Johnson (Brookings, Feb 2026) frame as the labor-share-vs-capital-share question.
